title: Learning from Many: Partner Exposure and Team Familiarity in Fluid Teams
abstract: In services where teams come together for short collaborations, managers are often advised to strive for high team familiarity so as to improve coordination and consequently, performance. However, inducing high team familiarity by keeping team membership intact can limit workers’ opportunities to acquire useful knowledge and alternative practices from exposure to a broader set of partners. We introduce an empirical measure for prior partner exposure and estimate its impact (along with that of team familiarity) on operational performance using data from the London Ambulance Service. Our analysis focuses on ambulance transports involving new paramedic recruits, where exogenous changes in team membership enable identification of the performance effect. Specifically, we investigate the impact of prior partner exposure on time spent during patient pickup at the scene and patient handover at the hospital. We find that the effect varies with the process characteristics. For the patient pickup process, which is less standardized, greater partner exposure directly improves performance. For the more standardized patient handover process, this beneficial effect is triggered beyond a threshold of sufficient individual experience. In addition, we find some evidence that this beneficial performance impact of prior partner exposure is amplified during periods of high workload, particularly for the patient handover process. Finally, a counterfactual analysis based on our estimates shows that a team formation strategy emphasizing partner exposure outperforms one that emphasizes team familiarity by about 9.2% in our empirical context. This paper was accepted by Jay Swaminathan, operations management.

summary.oneLiner: In London ambulance crews, prior partner exposure speeds up scene and handover times, and a partner-exposure team strategy beats team familiarity by about 9.2%.
summary.overview: Managers often try to keep teams intact so members know each other well and coordinate better. This paper studies new paramedics at the London Ambulance Service, whose partners change because of a relief roster, and measures how widely each recruit has worked with different partners. The authors find that broader partner exposure directly speeds up patient pick-up at the scene, a less standardized process, while for the more standardized hospital handover it helps only once the recruit has enough individual experience. A counterfactual analysis suggests a strategy emphasizing partner exposure would outperform one emphasizing team familiarity by about 9.2% in this setting.
summary.question: Does prior exposure to a broader set of partners improve operational performance in fluid teams, and how do its benefits compare with those of team familiarity?
summary.method: Econometric panel regressions on ambulance transport records, with fixed effects for recruits, hospitals, and clinical conditions, and clustered standard errors. Partner exposure is measured with a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of a recruit's experience spread across prior partners. Exogenous partner changes from the relief roster support identification. The authors then run counterfactual predictions comparing two hypothetical team formation strategies.
summary.data: 5,773 ambulance transports staffed by 81 new recruits (recruited in 2011) together with one or more of 702 senior paramedics, covering the entire calendar year 2011 at the London Ambulance Service. Outcomes are scene time and handover time at accident and emergency departments. The sample includes 37 A&E departments.
findings: For patient pick-up at the scene (a less standardized process), greater prior partner exposure is associated with shorter scene times, consistent with H1. The authors report that the effect is stronger during high workload periods, but note this result is sensitive to how crew workload is controlled.

For patient handover at hospital (a more standardized process), greater partner exposure is associated with shorter handover times only for recruits with sufficient individual experience, consistent with H2.
The authors find some evidence that the handover benefit is amplified during periods of high workload, consistent with H4.
Team familiarity is associated with shorter scene and handover times, with a modest effect per joint transport.

In the counterfactual analysis, a partner exposure strategy is predicted to outperform a partner focus strategy at the scene by about 11% and at handover by about 5.5%. The authors report an overall improvement of about 9.2%.
The authors note that the results come from one setting and two processes, so they are indicative rather than definitive.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest managers balancing team familiarity against partner exposure should analyze employees' work histories (who has worked with whom, on what tasks, and with what performance), since such data is routinely captured by enterprise IT systems. They argue the right balance depends on the standardization of the task, and that partner exposure matters particularly in fluid teams where stable partnerships are hard to maintain. They also note that the speed gains could matter for patient outcomes in life-threatening cases.
